text:
Philip Rubin is a distinguished scholar and leader in the fields of embodied cognition, speech technology, and science policy. Born in 1949, he earned his BA in psychology and linguistics from Brandeis University in 1971 and his PhD in experimental psychology from the University of Connecticut in 1975, under the mentorship of Michael Turvey and others. Rubin’s research focuses on the biological and computational foundations of speech and language, particularly articulatory synthesis, speech perception, and the principles of embodied cognition. His work includes foundational contributions to the development of ASY (Haskins articulatory synthesis program) and SWS (Haskins sinewave synthesis program), which revolutionized the study of speech production and perception.
Throughout his career, Rubin has been deeply involved in science policy and advocacy. He served as Chair of the National Academies Board on Behavioral, Cognitive, and Sensory Sciences, a member of the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences (FABBS), and the President of FABBS. He has also held significant roles in the National Science Foundation (NSF), including serving as the NSF ex officio representative to the National Human Research Protection Advisory Committee and the Secretary's Advisory Committee on Human Research Protections. Rubin has been a vocal advocate for ethical considerations in research, particularly regarding human subjects, emerging technologies, and the protection of privacy and security in intelligence and law enforcement communities.
Rubin’s theoretical contributions include a dynamical systems perspective on speech, emphasizing the spatiotemporal coordination of articulatory gestures and the role of embodiment in speech production and perception. His work has also explored the ethical implications of technological advancements, including concerns about the misuse of voice stress technologies and the broader implications of artificial intelligence and automation. He has been involved in numerous advisory roles, including serving as a judge for the DARPA Robotics Challenge, a participant in the White House Foster Care and Technology Hackathon, and a member of the NASA Advisory Council.
Rubin has received numerous honors and awards, including fellowships from the Acoustical Society of America, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and the Association for Psychological Science. He has also been recognized for his leadership in science policy and his contributions to the understanding of human speech and cognitive processes. His work bridges the gap between scientific research and public policy, advocating for the responsible and ethical development of technology and its applications.
